# Domains and borders {#sec-borders}

::: {.callout-note}
This chapter is planned: it states the question and the method. Results will replace the plan as the
analysis is done.
:::

Where two colour regions meet is where most of the action is. In physics, the boundaries between regions
(magnetic domains, soap foam, alloys) move by simple rules, and the rules differ between systems.

## The question

Do borders on the canvas behave like physical interfaces? Two textbook pictures predict different things
(*established* theory; see @sec-reading):

- In the **voter model**, where each site copies a random neighbour, borders stay rough and move without regard to
  their shape.
- In **curvature-driven** systems (Ising-like), sharp convex corners erode and concave notches fill in.

## Why it matters

Flags make this testable. Their intended shapes are known (straight edges, right angles, a few curves), so damage can
be measured against the intended outline. Two questions follow, both *speculative but testable*:

1. Does border motion depend on local curvature?
2. Does geometry change **maintenance cost**, the placements per unit time per unit border length needed to hold a
   shape? On a pixel grid a diagonal is a staircase of exposed corners, so it may cost more than a straight edge.

## Plan and cautions

- Colour domains as connected regions of one colour; border length and border velocity over time.
- Curvature on a pixel grid is noisy and angle-dependent, so borders are smoothed and results checked against the
  smoothing scale.
- Popular artworks attract defenders whatever their shape; comparisons control for size and neighbours.
